verdicts.reason: REFUTED on its load-bearing sentence, even though its line cites are verbatim-exact. The transform at :300/:318 is real and general — I read it — but it is territory↔SECTOR, not territory↔ROOM. The finding bridges that gap with an assertion in capitals, 'A SECTOR IS A ROOM, ONE TO ONE', and the SAME FILE contradicts it: :1434-1436 pushes the outer room as roomid 0 into a roomDataVector and then, when hasMoreRooms, keeps generating INNER rooms into that same vector; :1464-1480 hands the vector to createDungeon/createTempleDungeon/createCave/createMine/createRuins; :1710 indexes 'getNodeData(nodeid).getRoomData()[roomid]'. One node/sector therefore owns an ARRAY of rooms, and rooms carry their own 8-bit id space at :1791-1795, distinct from the nodeid's 12-bit packing. The second consequence is that the finding's ledger surgery would INTRODUCE an error: RR:224 already lists 'territory/sector coord system' under Ready, and RR:225 ① asks the further sector↔room question — so the ledger does not invert the vocabulary, and the pair the finding 'closes' is the pair already marked solved. Its stated refutation of 'one-screen-per-sector' is also a non-sequitur ('36 rooms per territory' is 36 SECTORS per territory); the real disproof is :1777, room width = 800 + rand(0..800), i.e. one to two 800 px screens. SALVAGE: the floor/mod-6 territory↔sector transform is genuine, general, and web-corroborated at §1t7785s0§.as:196-198 — keep that, discard the room identity and the RR:225 ① overturn.

new_findings.text: Found while checking nf1/nf2/nf3 in the same switch. The per-stance REACH table in §1t99s0§.as:3091-3155 is the mirror of the DAMAGE table at :3259-3271, and the ledger's 300/200/100 ordering is explained by it. Light (§1t12220s0§): damage ×(0.5+0.04·mLight) but reach ×1.4 FIXED (:3094). Balanced (§1t12221s0§): damage and reach BOTH ×(1+0.02·mBal) (:3105, :3265). Two further stance ids exist: §1t12223s0§ reach = base with the same 100 floor (:3142-3146) and §1t12224s0§ reach ×1.4 (:3131). So the stance that hits hardest reaches shortest, and each stance's reach is governed by its OWN mastery, not a shared one.
